title: Incremental stateful upgrade strategy for private deployments
author: Priya Nambiar
body:
Overview

Purpose: This document describes a repeatable, low-risk approach for performing incremental upgrades of stateful components in Redwood private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It covers the constraints that make private upgrades different from hosted upgrades, a staged upgrade pattern that avoids global halts, verification gates, rollback paths, and example commands and checklists for common stateful elements (KV cache, model shard sets, tokenizer/schema versions, and persistent infra).

Scope
- Applies to private deployments managed by Redwood control plane and customer-managed on-prem packages.
- Focus on runtime and stateful services: redwood-runtime pods (model servers), kv-cache service, redis/etcd clusters used for metadata, and the model artifact store.
- Excludes: control-plane-only service upgrades (covered in separate control-plane upgrade runbook).

Why incremental and state-aware?
- Stateful elements (KV caches, shard layouts, tokenizer mappings) cannot be replaced with a single rolling restart without risk of data-loss, cache poisoning, or model mismatch.
- Private environments are heterogeneous (different k8s versions, storage backends, network topologies) so deterministic, observable gates are required.

Roles and ownership
- Service Owner: engineering (serving-runtime team) — primary for upgrade coordination.
- Onsite Customer Lead: customer-appointed engineer — validation authority for private on-prem steps.
- SRE Oncall: supports traffic routing and emergency rollback.
- Release Engineer: orchestrates staged artifacts, manifests, and release notes.

Pre-upgrade checklist (run this before scheduling)
1) Release artifacts verified: signed model artifacts, runtime container digests, and helm chart SHA.
2) Backup snapshots: metadata DB backup (etcd/dynamo snapshot) and model artifact store index export.
3) KV cache export (if enabled): persistent snapshot or export to object store.
4) Telemetry baseline capture: a 24–72 hour sample of request rate, p50/p95 latency, token cost, and error rate.
5) Smoke test suite created for the specific deployment (small prompt set + model checks).
6) Maintenance window and rollback window communicated to customer.

Staged upgrade pattern (recommended)
1) Canaryless Shadow & Validation (stage 0)
   - Deploy new runtime alongside existing in shadow mode (no production traffic). Use traffic mirroring if supported by the service mesh.
   - Validate behavior on mirrored traffic and smoke tests. Verify identical output signatures for deterministic layers (tokenizer version, JSON schema).
   - Duration: 1–3 hours depending on traffic volume.

2) Read-Only Model Warmup (stage 1)
   - Start new model replicas in read-only mode that attach to same artifact store but do not register for write-only KV promotion.
   - Allow KV cache population via warmup workload (synthetic queries) until memory/kv-hit-rate reaches expected thresholds.

3) Incremental Traffic Admission (stage 2)
   - Admit small percentage of production traffic (5–10%) to new replicas. Use routing policy: weighted routing by route ID or token bucket, not global switch.
   - Observe live SLOs for 30–60 minutes per increment. Typical increments: 5 -> 10 -> 25 -> 50 -> 100. Pause on any gate failure.

4) State Promotion (stage 3)
   - Promote new replicas to full read/write once KV consistency checks pass. Promotion is a single-step per shard group to avoid split-brain.
   - For distributed metadata (etcd), perform quorum-aware rolling upgrades: upgrade minority nodes first, verify cluster health, then majority.

5) Post-cutover validation (stage 4)
   - Run acceptance prompts, regression detection suite, and compare output distributions against baseline.
   - Keep previous version available for at least 4 hours for immediate rollback if necessary.

Gate criteria (must pass to continue)
- Functional: smoke tests pass (100% success) and critical API responses within schema and length limits.
- Latency: p95 increase <= +15% from baseline and absolute p95 <= 300ms for typical low-latency workloads (adjust per-customer SLO).
- Errors: 5xx rate < 0.5% and new error classes not exceeding historical frequency.
- Quality: automated evals on 200 prompt set show BLEU/ROUGE/semantic-similarity within configured regression thresholds (per-customer config).
- Resource: GPU memory usage within expected bounds and no OOMs observed for at least two cycles of peak traffic.

Rollback strategy (fast path and safe path)
- Fast path: immediate traffic-weight revert to previous stable replica group (weighted routing). This is the default first-step rollback and should complete within 1–2 minutes.
- Safe path: if data/schema migration happened (e.g., tokenizer mapping or model shard relocation), perform controlled rollback steps: 1) Quiesce writes to the migrated shard, 2) run reconciliation job to restore previous metadata from snapshot, 3) restore previous model index and restart earlier runtime. This can take 30–120 minutes depending on artifact sizes.

Upgrade patterns for common stateful elements
- KV Cache (local, warm-in-memory): always warm in shadow mode first. Never invalidate or flush global caches during promotion unless explicit compatibility requires it.
- Model shard sets: add new shard replicas and replicate weights (replicate-to-standby), then atomically switch shard ownership using orchestration mapping stored in metadata DB.
- Tokenizer/schema changes: support dual-schema mode; accept and normalize old and new tokens in runtime for 24–72 hours before enforcing migration.
- Persistent stores (object stores, nfs): prefer immutable artifact publishing and pointer swap semantics rather than in-place mutates.

Example commands and snippets
- Deploy new runtime (Helm) in shadow mode:

```bash
helm upgrade --install redwood-runtime-v2 ./charts/redwood-runtime \
  --set-image=registry.redwood.internal/redwood-runtime:v2.3.0 \
  --set shadowMode.enabled=true \
  --set replicas=2 \
  --namespace redwood-private
```

- Mirror traffic (Istio example): create VirtualService with mirror percentage 100% to shadow subset but no mirroring for write paths.

- Promote replica group weight (example using rictl — internal deployment tool):

```bash
rictl traffic-weight --service redwood-runtime --from old:100 --to new:5
rictl wait-gates --service redwood-runtime --timeout 15m --checks smoke,latency,errors
```

- Backup artifact store index (S3 example):

```bash
aws s3 cp s3://customer-artifacts/index.json s3://customer-artifacts/backups/index-$(date +%F).json
```

Compatibility table (reference)

| Component | Minimum supported runtime | Migration allowed in-place? | Recommended pattern |
|-----------|---------------------------:|---------------------------:|---------------------|
| KV cache (local) | runtime v2.0.0 | No (use warm shadow) | shadow + warm + weighted admit |
| Model shards | v1.8.0 | Partially (replicate then switch) | replicate-standby + atomic ownership swap |
| Tokenizer mapping | v2.1.0 | No (dual-schema recommended) | dual-schema + normalize layer |
| Metadata DB (etcd) | etcd 3.5+ | Yes (quorum-aware rolling) | minority-first rolling upgrade |

(If your editor renders tables poorly, the above is a canonical mapping; copy into docs for a formatted table.)

Monitoring and acceptance checks
- Tracing: ensure distributed traces include upgrade-version tag. Verify end-to-end traces for 20 representative requests.
- Metrics to watch (alert thresholds):
  - redwood.requests.p95 (alert if > baseline * 1.2 for 15m)
  - redwood.requests.error_rate (alert if > 0.5% sustained 5m)
  - redwood.kv.hit_rate (warn if drop > 10%)
  - node.oom.count (critical if any OOM observed)

- Automated acceptance job: run redwood-eval with the customer prompt set and produce a results artifact stored in the deployment bucket. Example: "redwood-eval run --set customer-smoke --output s3://... --thresholds config.json"

Edge cases and known failure modes
- Incompatible tokenizer changes: if tokens reassign numeric ids, dual-schema normalization is mandatory.
- Partial shard transfer failure: if a replica fails during weight transfer, keep older replica active and abort promotion.
- Long artifact pulls in low-bandwidth sites: presign and prefetch artifacts to local cache nodes during stage 0.

Operational playbook (quick reference)
1) Start shadow deployment and warm caches. 2) Confirm baseline metrics and gate checks. 3) Admit 5% traffic for 30m; if gates pass, ramp to 25% then 50% then 100%. 4) Promote stateful components one shard-group at a time. 5) Monitor for 4 hours post-100% before marking release as stable. 6) If rollback required, perform fast-weight revert; if data migration performed, follow safe rollback steps.

Post-upgrade actions
- Update runbook with observed deviations and RCA if any gate failed.
- Run a full reconciliation job to validate that all model artifacts are referenced only by expected runtimes.
- Schedule a follow-up with the customer lead to confirm acceptance and close the change ticket.

Appendix: Troubleshooting snippets
- Force traffic reroute to older pods (kubectl example):

```bash
kubectl patch svc redwood-runtime -n redwood-private -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"v1"}}}'
```

- Evict a problematic node gracefully:

```bash
nodename=$(kubectl get nodes --selector=redwood-node=true -o name | head -n1)
kubectl drain $nodename --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120
```

- Recreate a KV cache from snapshot:

```bash
redwood-kv restore --snapshot s3://backups/kv-snap-2027-02-15.tar.gz --namespace redwood-private
```
